title: API Gateway + Orchestration: ownership sketch and interface matrix
body:
Context: quick sketch for how the API edge (API Gateway), the orchestration/control plane, and the runtime adapters should divide responsibilities and how routing policies should be expressed for multi-region deployments. This is intentionally lightweight: goal is to align service boundaries before we draft a formal ownership map and update the service catalog.

Background / problem statement:
- We have overlaps between the gateway team and control plane over: auth/enforcement, path-based routing, model variant fallbacks, and global failover logic.
- Runtime adapters (GPU pool connectives, on-prem connectors) need a clear contract for routing and capacity signals.
- Multi-region deployments require a simple policy surface for product teams to express latency, cost, and data residency preferences.

Goals for this doc:
- Define a minimal, practical split of responsibilities ("who owns what") for the next quarter.
- Provide a small interface matrix that teams can implement quickly.
- Outline routing policy primitives we can expose in service configs and the Console.

Assumptions:
- API Gateway = the edge L7 proxy that terminates customer traffic and performs auth, rate limits, and perimeter validation.
- Control Plane / Orchestration = central service that manages routing decisions at inbound request time, rolling deploys, canaries, and policy evaluation.
- Runtime Adapters = adapters that speak to distinct execution environments (hosted GPU pools, dedicated, private VPC) and expose capacity & health signals.

Ownership sketch (high level):
- API Gateway (team: eng-console-orchestration): owns TLS, JWT/OIDC verification, rate limit enforcement at the edge, request shaping (size limits), request-level observability tags, and basic path-level routing to the control plane. Responsible for initial request validation and blocking malformed/malicious requests.
- Control Plane / Orchestration (team: eng-platform): owns model routing logic, rollout policies (canary, A/B, percentage rollouts), fallback rules (model family fallbacks), global routing decisions, and persisting per-customer routing preferences. Exposes a small routing API consumed by the Gateway.
- Runtime Adapters (team: eng-serving-runtime + eng-private-deployments): own the runtime-side admission (accepting tasks), local healthchecks, capacity reporting, adapter-side rate shaping (to avoid OOMs on a node), and serving-side logs/metrics. They implement the control plane adapter contract and handle adapter-level failover (e.g., local replica restart).

Interface matrix (what each component exposes):
- API Gateway -> Control Plane:
  - call: RouteResolve(request_metadata) -> {route_id, preferred_region, fallback_chain, cache_key_opt_in}
  - semantics: synchronous, sub-10ms p95 target for local region lookups (cached responses allowed). Gateway caches RouteResolve results for TTL based on route stability metadata.
- Control Plane -> Gateway:
  - push: PolicyChange notifications (webhook / pubsub) for global rollout changes.
  - read: Administrative APIs for per-customer routing config, constraints, quotas.
- Control Plane -> Runtime Adapters:
  - RPC: OfferTask(task_descriptor) -> {accepted, estimated_latency, queue_token}
  - RPC: QueryCapacity() -> {gpu_slots, memory_headroom, region_affinity}
  - async: Health & metrics stream (prometheus pushgateway / OTLP).
- Runtime Adapters -> Control Plane:
  - provide durable capacity events and soft-eviction signals; implement a "grace_period" contract for in-flight KV cache reclamation.

Routing policy primitives (what product teams can set):
- latency_priority: high | medium | low (guides region affinity and whether to prefer warm cache hits)
- cost_tier: express intent (economy | balanced | premium) which can bias quantized variants and batch sizes
- data_residency: region code(s) or "any" (strict enforcement by control plane + gateway guardrails)
- availability_tier: standard | prioritized (controls failover order and preemptible usage)
- canary_spec: {percent, duration_minutes, metric_watchlist} (control plane handles rollout scheduling)
- fallback_policy: prefer_model_variant | prefer_region | degrade_to_analytic (explicit fallback chain semantics)

Multi-region specifics / constraints:
- Region affinity: control plane computes "preferred_region" using latency SLO + data_residency + runtime capacity signals. Gateway should bias routing to preferred_region but allow immediate fallthrough based on explicit policy.
- Cache affinity: prefix KV caches are region-local. When data_residency is strict, control plane will restrict route resolution to that region; otherwise it may route to a nearby region and set cache_key_opt_in=false to avoid cross-region cache poisoning.
- Cross-region failover: ordered list (primary -> warm standby -> cold fallback). Warm standby must have replicated model weights or fast cold-start policy. The control plane should maintain per-route replicated artifact metadata.

Operational responsibilities and SLOs (draft):
- Gateway: p99 request accept < 15ms (local), auth failures < 0.1% of valid requests, rate-limit correctness 99.99%
- Control plane: RouteResolve p95 < 25ms for cached lookups, < 100ms for cold lookups; Policy change propagation <= 5s to gateways for critical flag flips.
- Runtime Adapters: advertise capacity within 30s, health heartbeat < 60s; task acceptance latency < 50ms.

Adapter contract details (practical notes):
- Adapters must include: adapter_id, region_tags, supported_model_variants, max_concurrent_requests, graceful_drain_seconds.
- When under memory pressure, adapter should emit a "throttle_hint" that control plane can use to reduce routing to that adapter for N seconds.
- Private adapters (on-prem) must implement a separate auth handshake (mTLS + attestation token) and expose a smaller surface for route resolution to preserve customer network boundaries.

Edge cases and unresolved questions (todo / open):
- Who enforces per-customer data residency when private deployments exist for the same customer? (Control plane should prefer private adapter, but we need policy to prevent accidental spillover.)
- What is the canonical source of truth for route-level cache TTLs? Gateway or Control Plane? (Prefer control plane with gateway override guardrails.)
- How should we express "soft-cost" preferences for model variants? Current cost_tier is a blunt instrument; need more granular CPU/GPU preference bits.
- How do we coordinate cross-team SRE ownership for multi-region disaster runbooks? (Propose a rotating cross-team on-call for "global routing incidents".)

Migration approach (next 3 months):
- Week 1-3: Align owners and publish a short API spec (RouteResolve + PolicyChange) in Confluence.
- Week 4-6: Implement Gateway client cache rules and stub Control Plane RouteResolve endpoint (feature-flagged).
- Week 7-10: Instrument runtime adapters to emit capacity signals and throttle_hint.
- Week 11-12: Trial with two non-critical customers for multi-region routing with canary policies.

Action items (owners):
- Priya: publish API sketch and create Confluence page (PLAT-API-GW-OVERVIEW).
- Marco: prototype RouteResolve cache implementation in gateway (PR-198).
- Evelyn: add capacity reporting schema to runtime-adapter spec and update adapters.
- Samir: draft cross-region runbook and incident playbook.

Quick links / references:
- Confluence: PLAT-API-GW-OVERVIEW (work in progress)
- Jira: PLAT-4723 (routing policy primitives epic)
- Github: PR-198 (gateway cache client)

Notes to self / freeform thoughts:
- Keep the control plane surface intentionally small: route resolution + rollout control + policy store. Anything that requires per-request heavy lifting (token introspection of large claims sets, heavy transforms) should live in the gateway or a dedicated middleware.
- Consider adding a "cost_estimate" optional field in RouteResolve so caller (gateway) can tag request for telemetry. This will make later unit-cost attributions easier.

If we align on ownership here, I can synthesize a formal ownership map JSON for the service catalog and submit a PR to platform-ownership repo. For now this is a sketch to get buy-in.
